weak-field-limit-condition.title: Weak-Field Limit Condition
weak-field-limit-condition.conceptual_definition: This condition specifies the regime where the gravitational potential energy per unit mass is much smaller than the square of the speed of light, indicating a weak gravitational field.
weak-field-limit-condition.intuitive_summary: When this condition holds, gravity is weak, and spacetime is nearly flat, allowing for approximations where general relativity simplifies to Newtonian gravity.
weak-field-limit-condition.interpretation:
The condition $\Phi/c^2 \ll 1$ is fundamental for the weak-field approximation in general relativity. It implies that the gravitational field is not strong enough to significantly curve spacetime, and velocities are non-relativistic. Under this condition, the metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ can be approximated as the Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu
u}$ plus a small perturbation $h_{\mu
u}$, i.e., $g_{\mu
u} \approx \eta_{\mu
u} + h_{\mu
u}$, where $|h_{\mu
u}| \ll 1$. This approximation allows the Einstein Field Equations to be linearized, leading to a simplified set of equations that, in the appropriate limit, recover Newton's law of universal gravitation. It is the mathematical basis for understanding phenomena like gravitational lensing and gravitational waves in the weak-field regime.
weak-field-limit-condition.symmetry_origin: While general relativity is founded on the principle of general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance), the weak-field limit does not introduce new fundamental symmetries. Instead, it allows for approximations where the local spacetime geometry is nearly flat, making the Poincaré symmetry (Lorentz invariance and translational invariance) of special relativity a very good local approximation. The condition itself is a statement about the magnitude of a component of the metric perturbation relative to the speed of light, rather than a direct consequence of a symmetry principle.
weak-field-limit-condition.limits_and_boundary: This condition defines the Newtonian limit of general relativity. When $\Phi/c^2 \ll 1$, the equations of general relativity reduce to those of Newtonian gravity. It is valid far from massive objects, inside planets, or in systems with relatively low gravitational potential energy (e.g., the solar system). Conversely, when $\Phi/c^2 \sim 1$ or $\Phi/c^2 > 1$, the weak-field approximation breaks down, and the full non-linear Einstein Field Equations are required, such as near black holes or in the early universe.

Phi.name: Gravitational Potential
Phi.description: The Newtonian gravitational potential, typically negative, representing the potential energy per unit mass due to gravity.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the speed at which all electromagnetic radiation propagates in vacuum.
